title: Helio Health - technical deep dive: Splunk HEC for audit export (beta)
summary: Deep dive on Redwood’s SIEM-ready audit export beta focused on Splunk HEC delivery: endpoint/auth (token), recommended index/source/sourcetype, event format and mapping, batching/compression, rate limiting and 429/backoff behavior, delivery semantics (at-least-once + downstream dedup via event_id), and a proposed validation plan in Helio’s Splunk Cloud. Helio shared initial volume estimates and constraints (Splunk token scoping, index naming, expected throttles during business hours).
topics: Splunk HEC endpoint selection (/services/collector/event) and token handling
Payload shape: canonical audit schema v2, event_id, timestamps, category/action
Index, source, sourcetype conventions; CIM-ish mapping guidance
Throttling: Splunk 429 behavior, Redwood backoff, circuit breaker, max lag
Delivery semantics: at-least-once, dedup expectation, replay/backfill window
Customer validation plan: test connection, count reconciliation, outage simulation
questions: Can Redwood support Splunk HEC ACK (/services/collector/ack) for stronger delivery confirmation, or is beta best-effort on 200 responses?
What’s the max batch size (events and bytes) Redwood will send to Splunk before splitting?
How should Helio deduplicate in Splunk searches—by event_id alone or (event_id, tenant)?
Can Helio restrict Redwood egress to specific Splunk Cloud HEC hosts/allowlist?

next_steps: Helio to create Splunk HEC token + dedicated index (e.g., redwood_audit) and share endpoint + token via Redwood Console secret flow.
Redwood to enable beta flag for Helio tenant once config is ready (allowlist).
Run a 60–90 minute validation window: compare Redwood ‘events exported’ vs Splunk indexed counts; verify key fields and dashboards.
Schedule follow-up to review throttling behavior and adjust batching/backoff if Splunk rate limits are hit.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: Helio Health - technical deep dive: Splunk HEC for audit export (beta)
Date: 2025-03-18
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees (Redwood Inference): Colin O'Donnell, Simran Kaur, Benji Okafor
Attendees (Helio Health): Jenna Park, Miguel Alvarez, Rita Shah, Alex Chen

---

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for joining. This one is intended to be pretty tactical on Splunk HEC. We can stay out of the broader “what is the beta” stuff unless we need to.

[00:10] Simran Kaur: Yep. And for context we’re talking about the SIEM-ready audit export beta. Helio is on the shortlist, so this is basically making sure the integration is going to work end to end.

[00:20] Jenna Park: Sounds good. We mostly want to know, like, what hits Splunk, what format, and what happens when Splunk yells at you with 429s.

[00:28] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah and also, we’re Splunk Cloud. We’ve been burned by vendors that assume they can just blast HEC. So I want to be explicit about batch sizes and retries.

[00:40] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. We’ll cover that. Benji’s also here from control plane side if we get into config knobs.

[00:48] Benji Okafor: Hey everyone.

[00:50] Rita Shah: Hi.

[00:52] Alex Chen: Hi, thanks.

[01:00] Colin O'Donnell: Let me start with the “wire” basics. For Splunk we send to HEC, the event endpoint, so typically it’s https://<hec-host>:8088/services/collector/event. We use the Splunk token you generate. TLS in transit, obviously.

[01:18] Miguel Alvarez: Right, in Cloud it’s not always 8088, sometimes it’s a managed hostname. But okay.

[01:24] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, and one of the steps is you tell us the exact host. In our UI you’ll configure destination type “Splunk HEC,” then you paste the URL and then you provide the HEC token as a secret reference.

[01:38] Jenna Park: When you say secret reference, you mean you’re not storing it in plain text in the config?

[01:43] Benji Okafor: Correct. Config has a credential ref. Secret lives in our secrets store, encrypted at rest. RBAC around who can set/rotate it. And we redact it from logs.

[01:55] Jenna Park: Okay.

[01:56] Colin O'Donnell: Payload wise, we send JSON. Splunk HEC expects a wrapper: {"time": <epoch>, "host": ..., "source": ..., "sourcetype": ..., "index": ..., "event": {...}}. Our “event” is the canonical audit event schema v2.

[02:15] Rita Shah: Is that the one with an event ID?

[02:18] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. event_id is stable and unique per emitted audit event. That’s the main dedup key.

[02:26] Alex Chen: Unique globally or within tenant?

[02:30] Colin O'Donnell: Globally unique-ish, but practically you should treat it as unique within tenant/workspace. We include tenant_id/workspace_id fields, so if you want belt and suspenders, you can dedup on both.

[02:44] Miguel Alvarez: What are you putting in “host” field? Splunk uses that sometimes.

[02:48] Colin O'Donnell: Default is “redwood” or “redwood-inference” as host. But we can set it to something consistent like your workspace slug. In beta I think it’s a static value, but we can confirm.

[03:03] Benji Okafor: Yeah today it’s “redwood-inference” and we set “source” and “sourcetype” based on the destination config.

[03:10] Miguel Alvarez: Okay so we can set sourcetype = redwood:audit?

[03:13] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. Common pattern: source=redwood:audit, sourcetype=redwood:audit, index=whatever you want, e.g. “sec_audit” or “redwood_audit.”

[03:24] Jenna Park: We’ll want a dedicated index. Probably “vendor_redwood_audit.”

[03:29] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, I can do that.

[03:32] Colin O'Donnell: Great. On schema: required fields include event_id, occurred_at (timestamp), actor (type/id), action, resource (type/id), and a category taxonomy. Optional fields like source_ip and user_agent appear only when relevant and allowed. We also have PII redaction rules so we avoid dumping prompt contents or anything like that.

[03:56] Jenna Park: I’m going to ask the annoying question: do you ever put customer content in audit logs?

[04:01] Colin O'Donnell: No model inputs/outputs. Audit logs are about “who did what,” like API key created, role changed, export config updated, that kind of thing. For request-level stuff we’re careful—like we’ll log that an API key was used, but not the payload.

[04:18] Alex Chen: And what about IP addresses? Are those considered PII for your purposes?

[04:23] Colin O'Donnell: We treat them as sensitive. For some events, we include source_ip and user_agent, but the policy is “only when applicable” and where it’s needed for security ops. We can also offer redaction/minimization defaults; we’re not dumping full headers.

[04:42] Jenna Park: That’s fine; security wants IP.

[04:45] Miguel Alvarez: I want to talk throughput. What’s the expected volume from Redwood to us?

[04:50] Rita Shah: Yeah. We did a back-of-the-napkin. We’ve got around 300 engineers, maybe 100 active Redwood users, but API usage is high. Not sure audit events per token though.

[05:02] Colin O'Donnell: Important point: these are audit events, not request logs. So it’s not “one per inference call.” It’s per administrative action and some security events. For most customers, volume is more like hundreds to low thousands per day, not millions.

[05:18] Jenna Park: Wait, so no “every API call is an audit event”?

[05:21] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. We have a few categories like authentication events, API key usage anomalies, config changes, access policy changes. But not every completion request.

[05:33] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. Because HEC scaling in Cloud—if you try to do per-request logs it gets expensive.

[05:41] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. For your environment, what’s the thing you most need? Admin changes, access, exports.

[05:49] Alex Chen: Compliance wants evidence of admin changes and access controls. Security wants sign-in events and “API key created/rotated” type stuff.

[06:00] Colin O'Donnell: Great, that aligns.

[06:04] Miguel Alvarez: Still, even if it’s small volume, Splunk sometimes returns 429 if you’re too bursty. How do you batch?

[06:12] Colin O'Donnell: We batch multiple audit events per HEC request. We also gzip compress the payload. We have an internal queue and checkpointing, so if Splunk is down, we don’t drop the events; we retry with exponential backoff.

[06:28] Miguel Alvarez: How big is a batch? Like number of events or bytes.

[06:33] Colin O'Donnell: It’s size-based and time-based. I don’t want to quote a wrong number—Benji can confirm defaults, but think on the order of a few hundred events per post, capped by payload size.

[06:47] Benji Okafor: Defaults today: we cap at ~500 events or ~900KB uncompressed per request, whichever comes first. There’s also a flush interval so we don’t wait too long under low volume.

[07:02] Miguel Alvarez: Okay, that’s reasonable. Splunk likes smaller requests. 900KB uncompressed becomes, what, 150KB compressed depending.

[07:12] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. And if Splunk returns 429, we backoff. We also have a circuit breaker so we don’t hammer you. While circuit is open we queue.

[07:25] Jenna Park: Does that mean lag can grow?

[07:27] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. There’s an export lag metric we expose in Console and we alert internally. During beta we also have a “max lag safety” that can auto-pause if it’s getting pathological.

[07:41] Rita Shah: Auto-pause means you stop sending? Or you drop?

[07:44] Colin O'Donnell: Stop sending, keep queued. Then you or we resume after addressing downstream issues. No dropping unless you exceed retention window.

[07:54] Alex Chen: What’s the retention window?

[07:56] Colin O'Donnell: For beta, we’re positioning backfill up to 7 days. We can do a manual backfill if needed. But it’s not infinite.

[08:07] Jenna Park: That’s fine.

[08:09] Miguel Alvarez: What about “HEC ACK”? Splunk has an acknowledgements feature. Do you support that? It’s not required but it’s nice.

[08:18] Colin O'Donnell: Today, for beta, we rely on HTTP response success and our own checkpointing. We don’t do HEC ack roundtrip yet.

[08:28] Miguel Alvarez: So you send, get 200, you consider it delivered.

[08:31] Colin O'Donnell: That’s right.

[08:34] Miguel Alvarez: That’s usually okay. Splunk Cloud is pretty consistent. The bigger issue is duplicates.

[08:39] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, and we are explicitly “at least once.” So duplicates are possible, especially around retries. That’s why event_id exists.

[08:48] Jenna Park: So in Splunk we dedup using event_id.

[08:50] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. And we can provide sample SPL: something like `... | stats dc(event_id) as unique count as total` and you can alert on total > unique by too much.

[09:05] Rita Shah: Does your exporter ever reorder events?

[09:08] Colin O'Donnell: It can. We preserve ordering per tenant stream as best effort, but with retries and batching, don’t rely on strict ordering. Use occurred_at.

[09:18] Alex Chen: Any guarantees on timestamps? Are they “when action happened” or “when exported”?

[09:23] Colin O'Donnell: occurred_at is when the action happened. exported_at we can add, but in Splunk you’ll see ingestion time and you’ll have occurred_at in the payload.

[09:35] Miguel Alvarez: Can you walk through 429 behavior in detail? Like initial delay and max.

[09:41] Colin O'Donnell: Sure. If we get 429, we treat it as retryable. Backoff with jitter. We also honor Retry-After if present.

[09:51] Benji Okafor: Splunk sometimes doesn’t send Retry-After; in that case we use exponential backoff starting at ~2 seconds, doubling up to a few minutes max. Circuit opens after consecutive failures.

[10:05] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. In Cloud, sometimes we get 503 too.

[10:09] Colin O'Donnell: Same handling: retryable.

[10:12] Jenna Park: What happens if our token gets revoked, like 403.

[10:16] Colin O'Donnell: That’s non-retryable until you rotate credentials. We surface it as destination unhealthy. We stop spamming with retries after a threshold and we mark the destination as error.

[10:29] Rita Shah: So it won’t keep trying forever and fill your queue?

[10:32] Colin O'Donnell: Correct, that’s the point of the circuit breaker / pause. We still keep queued events within window.

[10:41] Jenna Park: Are you validating the destination host to prevent, like, SSRF? Sorry, security brain.

[10:47] Benji Okafor: Yes. We validate hostname and scheme. There’s an egress allowlist system. For Splunk Cloud it’s typically your known HEC domain(s). We can also restrict to 443 if you have that.

[11:02] Miguel Alvarez: Our HEC is on 443, yeah. Not 8088.

[11:05] Colin O'Donnell: Great, we’ll use whatever URL you provide.

[11:09] Simran Kaur: Maybe we should outline a concrete validation plan so everyone knows what “done” looks like.

[11:14] Jenna Park: Yes please.

[11:16] Colin O'Donnell: Proposed plan:
1) You create an index, set up a HEC token with permissions limited to that index.
2) In Redwood Console, you create destination with URL, token, index/source/sourcetype.
3) Run “test connection” from Console. That sends a single synthetic event (non-sensitive) and we verify Splunk 200.
4) Then we enable real audit stream and let it run for, say, an hour.
5) You validate fields in Splunk: event_id, occurred_at, actor, action, category, tenant/workspace.
6) Then we simulate throttling by temporarily lowering HEC limits or just observing during a known busy period; we confirm our backoff doesn’t explode your intake.
7) Finally, we do a controlled pause/resume to demonstrate catch-up (lag goes up then down) and confirm no data loss, only possible dupes.

[12:08] Miguel Alvarez: For step 3, the synthetic event, does it use the same sourcetype/index settings?

[12:13] Colin O'Donnell: Yep.

[12:14] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[12:16] Alex Chen: For compliance we’ll want a screenshot or export of sample events with the fields, and also a statement on retention vs export responsibilities.

[12:28] Simran Kaur: We have an internal FAQ we can share (sanitized) that describes that Redwood retains audit logs for a defined period and export is for you to retain in your SIEM. We’ll provide language.

[12:40] Jenna Park: Okay.

[12:42] Rita Shah: On filtering—can we limit to certain categories? Like only “access” and “admin” at first.

[12:49] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. In the export config, there’s a filter builder. You can allowlist categories and actions. Recommended to start broader, but if you want to reduce noise, we can do allowlist.

[13:03] Miguel Alvarez: Splunk cost is basically ingestion, so yeah, we want to avoid junk.

[13:08] Colin O'Donnell: Understood. Typical categories are “authn”, “authz”, “admin”, “resource”, “billing” (depending), and “export”. We can send you the full list.

[13:23] Jenna Park: We definitely want export config changes logged.

[13:26] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, those are first-class audit events.

[13:30] Miguel Alvarez: Any chance your exporter sends multiline JSON? Because Splunk sometimes gets weird.

[13:35] Colin O'Donnell: It’s one JSON per HEC event wrapper. Over the wire it’s standard. In Splunk you’ll see the JSON in _raw, but it’s parseable.

[13:46] Rita Shah: Do you set “fields” in HEC? Splunk has a “fields” attribute.

[13:50] Colin O'Donnell: Not in beta. We rely on extracting from event JSON. But we can align with Splunk CIM-ish naming in the payload.

[14:03] Miguel Alvarez: We can do props/transforms to extract. Fine.

[14:06] Colin O'Donnell: Great. On dedup, we recommend you extract event_id as a field and then use it in correlation searches.

[14:16] Jenna Park: If there’s duplicates, is it usually just the same event resent? Or can it be partial batches?

[14:23] Colin O'Donnell: Usually whole-batch resend after timeout or ambiguous response. So you might see a chunk repeated. That’s why event_id is per event.

[14:35] Miguel Alvarez: Makes sense.

[14:36] Colin O'Donnell: Now, Helio-specific: what’s your expected audit event volume? Even rough.

[14:43] Jenna Park: Hard to say. Maybe 5k/day? But that’s based on other SaaS audit logs.

[14:48] Rita Shah: Admin actions are low. Auth events could be higher if you log every SSO. But still not insane.

[14:56] Colin O'Donnell: Great, 5k/day is nothing for this system.

[15:00] Miguel Alvarez: But we might burst if there’s an incident and people do a bunch of key rotations.

[15:04] Colin O'Donnell: Right. Our batching and backoff covers burst. Also, the exporter is per-tenant isolated so you won’t be impacted by other tenants, and vice versa.

[15:16] Benji Okafor: And on our side we have per-destination rate limiting too, so we don’t exceed configured request rate.

[15:23] Miguel Alvarez: Is that configurable?

[15:25] Benji Okafor: In beta it’s mostly defaults, but we can tune for specific customers.

[15:31] Jenna Park: Can we do a “dry run” first? Like only synthetic events.

[15:35] Colin O'Donnell: We can do test connection and then keep it disabled until you’re ready. But once enabled, it’s real.

[15:43] Alex Chen: We’ll need to coordinate with change control.

[15:46] Simran Kaur: Totally. We can plan a window.

[15:50] Miguel Alvarez: Security question: do you support mTLS?

[15:54] Colin O'Donnell: Not for Splunk HEC in beta. It’s token + TLS.

[16:00] Jenna Park: Okay.

[16:02] Rita Shah: How do you handle multi-region? We’re mostly in us-east.

[16:06] Colin O'Donnell: Exporter runs in the same region as your Redwood hosted workload. We’ll send from that region’s egress. That matters for allowlisting.

[16:16] Miguel Alvarez: That’s important. We allowlist IPs.

[16:19] Colin O'Donnell: We can provide a static egress range for the region for beta, or we can go through an allowlist mechanism. We’ll follow up with details.

[16:31] Jenna Park: Okay.

[16:34] Colin O'Donnell: Quick note: beta is feature-flagged. Once you’re ready, we’ll have Support enable the tenant allowlist. Then you can set configs.

[16:45] Simran Kaur: And we’ll do weekly check-ins for the first few weeks.

[16:49] Rita Shah: Good.

[16:50] Miguel Alvarez: Can you show an example event?

[16:52] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, I’ll read a simplified one. Like:
- event_id: “01HR…”
- occurred_at: “2025-03-18T16:45:12Z”
- category: “admin”
- action: “api_key.create”
- actor: {type: “user”, id: “usr_…”, email_hash: “…”}
- resource: {type: “api_key”, id: “key_…”, name: null}
- request: {source_ip: “x.x.x.x”, user_agent: “…”}
We don’t include the API key value, obviously.

[17:26] Jenna Park: You said email hash?

[17:28] Colin O'Donnell: In some contexts we hash or omit. Depends on event type and policy. We can discuss what you need for correlation.

[17:36] Alex Chen: For compliance, we need actor identity. Hash may not be enough.

[17:41] Colin O'Donnell: Understood. In product UI you’ll see full user, but in exported event we can include user_id and maybe email, but we need to align with our PII rules. We can follow up with Security for what’s allowed.

[17:56] Jenna Park: User_id is okay. Email is nice-to-have.

[18:00] Miguel Alvarez: Splunk correlation usually uses username/email. But we can join with your directory if needed.

[18:05] Rita Shah: We can map user_id to SSO subject if Redwood provides that.

[18:10] Colin O'Donnell: We typically have user_id and sometimes “actor.display_name”. Let’s confirm what’s in your tenant’s audit events.

[18:20] Simran Kaur: We should be careful not to over-promise on identity fields; we’ll confirm with Marcus/Security.

[18:28] Jenna Park: Totally.

[18:31] Miguel Alvarez: Another Splunk thing: HEC has “sourcetype” indexing time extraction. If your JSON is nested, we’ll need KV_MODE = json.

[18:39] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We recommend setting KV_MODE=json for that sourcetype.

[18:44] Miguel Alvarez: Great.

[18:46] Colin O'Donnell: Okay, last section: troubleshooting. Common errors:
- 401/403: token issues.
- 404: wrong endpoint path.
- 429: rate limiting.
- 5xx: transient.
We surface these in destination health, with last error and last success time.

[19:09] Rita Shah: Where do we see that? In Redwood Console?

[19:12] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, the export settings page includes status: last delivered event time, lag estimate, and recent errors.

[19:22] Jenna Park: Can we get metrics exported to our monitoring? Like Prometheus.

[19:26] Colin O'Donnell: Not in beta as a customer-facing metrics endpoint, but we can share the health status and also we can provide periodic reports. In GA we might do webhooks or metrics.

[19:40] Alex Chen: For incident response, we just need to know if it’s working.

[19:43] Colin O'Donnell: Yep.

[19:46] Miguel Alvarez: Is there a way to re-send if something went wrong? Like if we messed up sourcetype.

[19:52] Colin O'Donnell: There’s replay/backfill within the supported window. In beta it’s mostly operator-assisted. You’d open a support ticket and we can trigger replay from checkpoint.

[20:04] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[20:06] Jenna Park: I think the key remaining question is whether we need HEC ACK. For now I think we can accept at-least-once plus dedup.

[20:15] Alex Chen: As long as we can explain it in a control narrative.

[20:18] Simran Kaur: We can give you customer-facing wording: “at-least-once delivery; customers should deduplicate using event_id; exporter includes retry/backoff and operational visibility.”

[20:30] Miguel Alvarez: Works.

[20:31] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Let’s do quick recap and assign next steps.

[20:37] Colin O'Donnell: Miguel, you’ll create index and token, and send us the HEC endpoint hostname(s). Jenna, you’ll confirm internally on whether ACK is required. We’ll send you setup snippets and sample SPL for validation, and we’ll confirm the default backoff parameters.

[20:55] Miguel Alvarez: Yep.

[20:56] Jenna Park: Yes.

[20:58] Rita Shah: And we’ll schedule a change window for enabling.

[21:02] Simran Kaur: I’ll coordinate that.

[21:05] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. Any last questions?

[21:09] Miguel Alvarez: Not from me.

[21:10] Alex Chen: Nope.

[21:12] Jenna Park: All good.

[21:14] Colin O'Donnell: Cool, thanks all.
